hmmt-nov-2016-thm-01.title: Complement
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-01.body:
He scores nothing with probability $\left(\frac35\right)^2=\frac9{25}$, so he scores at least one point with probability $1-\frac9{25}=\frac{16}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac{16}{25}$**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-02.title: Each car travels 300 miles
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-02.body:
The first car needs $\frac{300}{50}=6$ hours, so they meet at $1{:}00$ PM. The second car started at $8{:}00$ AM and travelled $5$ hours, so $x=\frac{300}{5}=60$ miles per hour.

**Answer: 60**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-03.title: Reflect B in the bisector
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-03.body:
By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac46$, so $BD=2$, $DC=3$. Reflect $B$ across the bisector $AD$: the image $X$ lies on ray $AC$ with $AX=AB=4$, and $E$ (the foot of the perpendicular from $B$) is the midpoint of $BX$. In triangle $BXC$ the line through $E$ parallel to $XC$ (which lies along $AC$) passes through the midpoint of $BC$, so $F$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $BF=\frac52$. Then $DF=BF-BD=\frac52-2=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-04.title: Each number needs two primes
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-04.body:
Let the numbers be $w,x,y,z$ in order around the square, with $\gcd(w,y)=\gcd(x,z)=1$ and adjacent numbers not coprime. Pick a prime $p_{wx}$ dividing both $w$ and $x$, and similarly $p_{xy},p_{yz},p_{zw}$. Neighbouring primes are different (if $p_{wx}=p_{xy}$ then it divides both $w$ and $y$), and opposite ones are different ($p_{wx}\mid w$, $p_{yz}\mid y$ and $\gcd(w,y)=1$), so these four primes are distinct. Then $w\ge p_{zw}p_{wx}$, $x\ge p_{wx}p_{xy}$, and so on, so the sum is at least $p_{zw}p_{wx}+p_{wx}p_{xy}+p_{xy}p_{yz}+p_{yz}p_{zw}=(p_{zw}+p_{xy})(p_{wx}+p_{yz})$.

For four distinct primes the product of the two pair-sums is smallest when they are $2,3,5,7$ split as $\{2,3\},\{5,7\}$: $5\cdot12=60$ (the other splits give $7\cdot10=70$ and $9\cdot8=72$). It is attained by $10,15,21,14$: opposite numbers $10,21$ and $15,14$ are coprime, adjacent ones share $5,3,7,2$.

**Answer: 60**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-05.title: Condition on scoring
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-05.body:
A missed shot leaves the state unchanged, so only scoring events matter. Each flip scores $1$ with probability $\frac12$ (tails) and $3$ with probability $\frac14$ (heads and made); given that the flip scores, it is a $1$ with probability $\frac23$ and a $3$ with probability $\frac13$.

He hits exactly $5$ via the point sequences $1,1,1,1,1$ ($\left(\frac23\right)^5=\frac{32}{243}$), and $1,1,3$; $1,3,1$; $3,1,1$ (each $\frac13\cdot\frac49=\frac4{27}$). Total: $\frac{32}{243}+3\cdot\frac{4}{27}=\frac{32}{243}+\frac{108}{243}=\frac{140}{243}$.

**Answer: $\frac{140}{243}$**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-06.title: Factor and use symmetry
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-06.body:
$x^6+6x^3-216=(x^3-12)(x^3+18)$. The roots of $x^3=12$ are three points at modulus $\sqrt[3]{12}$, $120^\circ$ apart, and those of $x^3=-18$ are three points at modulus $\sqrt[3]{18}$, rotated by $60^\circ$. So the six points alternate in modulus around the origin at $60^\circ$ intervals. The hexagon splits into six triangles with sides $\sqrt[3]{12},\sqrt[3]{18}$ and an included $60^\circ$ angle, each of area $\frac12\sqrt[3]{216}\sin60^\circ=\frac12\cdot6\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. Total: $9\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $9\sqrt3$**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-07.title: Parity and a construction
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-07.body:
Write the sides as vectors $(x_i,y_i)$ with $\sum x_i=\sum y_i=0$. Since $a^2\equiv a\pmod2$, $\sum(x_i^2+y_i^2)\equiv\sum(x_i+y_i)=0\pmod2$: the sum of squared lengths is even.

The squared length of a lattice side is a sum of two squares: the smallest positive values are $1,2,4,5,8,9,10,13,\dots$. Seven distinct sides use seven distinct values; the seven smallest sum to $1+2+4+5+8+9+10=39$ (odd), and no seven distinct values sum to $40$ (that would mean raising one of the seven values by exactly $1$, giving $2,3,5,6,9,10$ or $11$; but $2,5,9,10$ are already used and $3,6,11$ are not sums of two squares). The sum must be even, so it is at least $42$, attained by replacing $10$ with $13$.

Construction: $(0,0),(3,0),(5,1),(6,2),(3,4),(2,4),(0,2)$ is a convex heptagon with squared sides $9,5,2,13,1,8,4$, which are distinct and sum to $42$.

**Answer: 42**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-08.title: Count crossings for each step
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-08.body:
For $i=1$ and $i=7$ the red lines are the sides: $0$ crossings. For $i=2$ and $i=6$ the lines form two squares crossing: $8$ crossings. For $i=3$ and $i=5$ they form the star $\{8/3\}$: $16$ crossings. For $i=4$ they are the four long diagonals: $\binom42=6$ crossings. The expected number is $\frac{0+8+16+6+16+8+0}{7}=\frac{54}7$ (counts confirmed by computer).

**Answer: $\frac{54}7$**

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-09.title: Three colours and count
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-09.body:

Colour $1,4,7$ with $A,B,C$ ($3!=6$ ways, by symmetry say $1=A$, $4=B$, $7=C$). Vertex $2$ is next to $1$, so $2

So $n=6\cdot3=18$ and $mn=3\cdot18=54$ (confirmed by computer).

hmmt-nov-2016-thm-10.title: Invariant: total position value
hmmt-nov-2016-thm-10.body:
Give a chip on $A_i$ the value $i$, and let the total value be the sum over chips. The first move changes the value by $-2i+(i+1)=-(i-1)\le0$ (no change only at $A_1$), and the second move by $-2(i+1)+(i+2)+i=0$. So the total never increases and starts at $n$.

*$n=46$ works.* Use only value-preserving moves (the second type, and the first type on $A_1$). The sum of squares of positions strictly increases with each such move and the value is fixed, so the process must stop. At the end no move is available, so every position $A_1,\dots,A_9$ has at most one chip (two chips on $A_j$, $j\le9$, can always be moved). If $A_{10}$ were empty, the total value would be at most $1+2+\cdots+9=45<46$, a contradiction. So a chip reaches $A_{10}$.

*$n\le45$ fails.* Reaching $A_{10}$ requires moves removing two chips from each of $A_1,\dots,A_9$. Look at the last such move at $A_k$ ($2\le k\le9$): afterwards nothing moves past $A_k$ again, so a chip left on $A_{k-1}$ stays there; thus at the moment the chip on $A_{10}$ arrives, there are chips on $A_1,\dots,A_8$ as well, of total value at least $1+2+\cdots+8+10=46>n$. An exhaustive search of all reachable configurations confirms that $45$ chips never reach $A_{10}$ while $46$ do (and for $k$ points the minimum is $1+2+\cdots+(k-2)+k$).

**Answer: 46**
